newsitem.title: JAPAN: Expert suspects carbon dioxide killed Japan troops.
newsitem.headline: Expert suspects carbon dioxide killed Japan troops.

text.p: Three army soldiers who died of mysterious fumes during mountain training on a volcano in northern Japan may have succumbed to a freak carbon dioxide emission, a Japanese volcano expert said on Monday.

Volcanology Professor Junichi Hirabayashi of Tokyo Engineering University said air samples from a volcanic pit on the side of Mt Hakkoda where the soldiers collapsed showed concentrations of carbon dioxide 500 times the lethal level.

Hirabayashi said in a report to the army, or the Ground Self-Defence Force, that the soldiers may have died from the emission, or a combination of the emission and a lack of oxygen, an army spokesman said.
Army chemical warfare experts were analysing air and ground samples taken by Hirabayashi, the spokesman said.
Aomori prefectural police said the cause of death was still not clear and have decided to conduct autopsies.

The accident occurred on Mt Hakkoda, about 600 km (400 miles) north of Tokyo, on Saturday, the last day of a four-day survival training exercise by 23 infantrymen of the army's Ninth Division, headquartered in Aomori.

One soldier accidentally fell into an eight-metre-deep (25 ft) pit on the side of the volcano. The instructing officer climbed down into the pit to rescue him but the two became ill. Sixteen others followed and 12 of them collapsed.
The 12 were taken to hospital but three of them, aged 21 and 22, died.

The 1,585-metre (4,914-ft) volcano has a tragic link with Japan's military. In 1902, 199 army soldiers froze to death in a blizzard on the volcano during winter training, the worst military accident in modern Japan.
